messages.content:
For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

content.text:
As stated, this asks for a determination that is **not presently known**. In particular, the general implication defining \(S\) is an open Oka-complement problem.

The established complement theorem is that
\[
K\subset\mathbb C^n\ \text{compact and polynomially convex},\quad n\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\ \text{is Oka}.
\]
One cannot replace “polynomially convex” here by “the closure of a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain” as an established general theorem. Smooth pseudoconvexity does not imply polynomial convexity; it does not even guarantee a Stein neighbourhood basis. Thus this theorem does not determine \(S\) in the question.

There is a useful necessary implication in dimension two:
\[
2\in N.
\]
Indeed, if \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\), its Levi form is negative at some boundary point. With the orientation reversed, the complement has a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point. A local peak function there, truncated and extended by a constant, gives a nonconstant bounded plurisubharmonic function on the complement. An Oka manifold cannot admit such a function: convex approximation implies strong dominability, and bounded-above plurisubharmonic functions pulled back to \(\mathbb C^m\) are constant.

Consequently, the requested exact pair cannot currently be supplied without resolving an open problem:
\[
\boxed{\text{The exact ordered pair }(S,N)\text{ is not presently known.}}
\]

What they established:

## Established result and overall status

The team proved **\(2\in N\)**: if \(K\in\mathcal K_2\) and \(\mathbb C^2\setminus K\) is Oka in the stated CAP sense, then \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex.

They did **not** prove either remaining requirement for the supplied answer:
- for every \(n\ge2\), a pseudoconvex \(K\in\mathcal K_n\) with non-Oka complement;
- for every \(n\ge3\), a nonpseudoconvex \(K\in\mathcal K_n\) with Oka complement.

Nothing established contradicts \((S,N)=(\varnothing,\{2\})\). Several findings contradict proposed intermediate lemmas, not that answer.

## Complete proof of \(2\in N\)

The key general obstruction is that an Oka domain cannot have a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point, oriented from the domain’s side.

Write \(Y=\mathbb C^2\setminus K\). If \(K\) has a negative tangential Levi direction at \(q\), then, since the complex tangent is one-dimensional, \(Y\) is strongly pseudoconvex there. Let \(r<0\) define \(Y\) locally. In adapted unitary coordinates,
\[
H_r(q)=
\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&b\\\bar b&c\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \partial r(q)=(0,a),\qquad \lambda,a>0.
\]
Replacing \(r\) by \(r+Ar^2\) changes the lower-right entry at \(q\) to \(c+2Aa^2\). Its determinant is
\[
\lambda(c+2Aa^2)-|b|^2,
\]
so sufficiently large \(A\) makes the replacement strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\).

Shrink to a ball \(B_R(q)\), ensuring \(|Ar|<1/2\), and choose \(\eta>0\) sufficiently small that
\[
h=r+Ar^2-\eta\|z-q\|^2
\]
remains strictly psh. On \(Y\cap B_R(q)\), \(h\le-\eta\|z-q\|^2\). With \(c_0=\eta R^2/8\), glue
\[
\psi=\max(h,-c_0)
\]
inside the ball to the constant \(-c_0\) outside. The formulas already agree on the shell \(R/2\le\|z-q\|<R\). Thus \(\psi\) is globally bounded psh on \(Y\), and strictly psh on a nonempty open cap approaching \(q\).

For any entire \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\), bounded-psh Liouville makes \(\psi\circ F\) constant. If \(F\) meets the cap, strict positivity forces \(dF=0\) on a nonempty open set, hence \(F\) is constant. CAP applied to a nonconstant affine disk contained in the cap is therefore impossible: sufficiently close approximants must meet the cap, but constants cannot approximate its two distinct endpoint values arbitrarily well.

The proof is saved in **`workspace/agent3_dimension2_proof.txt`**. **`workspace/agent3_levi_check.py`** checks the universal defining-function Hessian chain identity, determinant calculation, and gluing margins.

## Additional proved tools and exclusions

### Solid-circle tori are not the desired counterexamples

For
\[
K_\varepsilon=\{(|z|^2-1)^2+\|w\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\},
\qquad 0<\varepsilon<1,
\]
the boundary is strongly pseudoconvex in every dimension. The nontrivial tangential Levi numerator, with \(t=|z|^2\), is
\[
2[t-(1-\varepsilon^2)]^2+2\varepsilon^2(1-\varepsilon^2)>0.
\]
See **`agent1_fat_torus_check.py`**.

More importantly, their complements are Oka, using standard density-property and Oka-localization theorems. The reusable lemma proved in **`workspace/agent2_shifted_pole_lemma.txt`** is:

> If compact \(K\) is holomorphically convex in \(\mathbb C^*\times\mathbb C^{n-1}\), then \(\mathbb C^n\setminus K\) is Oka.

For small nonzero \(a\), transfer convexity to \((\mathbb C\setminus\{a\})\times\mathbb C^{n-1}\). Points near the deleted hyperplane are separated by \(1/(z-a)\); elsewhere approximate original Laurent separators using
\[
1/z=\sum_{k\ge0}(-a)^k/(z-a)^{k+1}.
\]
Kusakabe’s compact-complement theorem applies in both density-property ambients, and the two resulting Zariski-open Oka sets cover the complement. Log-fiber concavity proves the initial Laurent convexity of \(K_\varepsilon\). **`agent4_shifted_pole_check.py`** checks the relevant identities.

### Explicit nonrationally-convex strongly pseudoconvex balls

Put
\[
h(z)=\frac{e^{2\pi i|z|^2}-1}{2\pi iz},
\]
smoothly extended at zero, and \(\varepsilon=1/(32\pi)\). In every dimension, the set
\[
K=\left\{|w-h(z)|^2+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}|z|^2+\|u\|^2
\le\varepsilon^2\right\}
\]
is a smooth strongly pseudoconvex topological ball. Here \(h_{\bar z}=e^{2\pi i|z|^2}\); the nontrivial Levi determinant is at least \(3/4+\varepsilon^2/4\).

The circle \((z,0,0)\), \(|z|=1\), lies inside \(K\), is nullhomotopic there, and bounds a flat analytic disk containing \(p=(1/2,0,0)\notin K\). The argument principle puts that disk in the rational hull. Checks are in **`agent1_graph_disk_check.py`**, **`agent2_nonrational_ball_check.py`**, and **`agent4_graph_ball_check.py`**.

**Non-Oka exteriors were not proved for these balls.** Nonrational convexity alone supplies no established bridge.

## Higher-dimensional candidates: geometry only

Two checked families remain possible leads:

- **Quartic:** \(K=\{\|z\|^2+|w|^4-|w|^2\le1\}\), \(z\in\mathbb C^{n-1}\). It is smooth, bounded, connected and nonpseudoconvex; its Levi matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(I,4|w|^2-1)\). See **`agent4_levi_check.py`**.
- **Sphere tube:** \(K_\varepsilon=\{(\|z\|^2-1)^2+|w|^2\le\varepsilon^2\}\), now \(z\in\mathbb C^{n-1}\). It is diffeomorphic to \(S^{2n-3}\times\overline B^3\). On its inner half the tangential signature is one positive and \(n-2\) negative eigenvalues. See **`agent3_sphere_tube_check.py`**.

Neither complement was proved Oka. Oka ball-complement fibers, affine lines, real-open unions of Oka domains, or curve-flexibility/Oka-1 criteria do not establish full CAP.

## Failed routes and reproducibility

Explicit Hénon escaping basins refute torus-based domination and “uniform Hartogs–Liouville” obstructions, even for fat solid-circle tubes. Exponential maps from \(\mathbb C^*\) realize proposed torus meridians. See **`agent2_obstruction_checks.py`** and **`agent4_fat_torus_escape.py`**.

**`agent2_three_section_countercheck.py`** refutes simple connected-fiber arguments with arbitrarily many parallel affine sections. **`agent3_proper_Cstar2.py`** supports an explicit ambient-proper entire curve into \((\mathbb C^*)^2\). Neither resolves the missing existence claims.

No reliable theorem was identified connecting Oka compact exteriors to the required proper analytic varieties, or proving arbitrary Hartogs/fiberwise-ball complements Oka. Worm and higher-rational-hull approaches remain conditional.

## Main result: the stipulated answer is contradicted

The team did **not** prove \((S,N)=(\mathbb Z_{\ge2},\varnothing)\). Instead, they established directly from the problem’s approximation definition that
\[
\boxed{2\in N.}
\]
Thus the prescribed conclusion \(N=\varnothing\) is false. Their argument does not determine the full pair \((S,N)\), and they proved no general forward implication establishing membership in \(S\).

## Complete argument establishing \(2\in N\)

The proof has two elementary analytic ingredients.

### 1. The stated Oka property forces bounded continuous plurisubharmonic functions to be locally constant

Let \(Y\) satisfy the problem’s Oka approximation property, and let \(u:Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, plurisubharmonic, and bounded above.

Take any sufficiently small affine disc
\[
f(\zeta)=p+\zeta v
\]
whose image on a neighbourhood of \(\overline{\mathbb D}\) lies in \(Y\). Applying the definition with \(m=1\) and \(Q=\overline{\mathbb D}\), obtain entire maps \(F_j:\mathbb C\to Y\) converging uniformly to \(f\) on \(\overline{\mathbb D}\).

Each \(u\circ F_j\) is a bounded-above subharmonic function on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant by subharmonic Liouville. Continuity of \(u\) gives, for every \(\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb D}\),
\[
u(f(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(0))
=u(f(0)).
\]
Therefore \(u\) is constant on every sufficiently small affine disc, and so locally constant on \(Y\). No connectedness assumption on the whole exterior is needed.

### 2. A strictly pseudoconvex boundary point produces a forbidden bounded psh function

Suppose \(Y\) has a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point \(q\). Choose a local defining function \(r\) with \(Y=\{r<0\}\) near \(q\), and translate \(q\) to \(0\).

Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(\ker\partial r(0)\) implies that, for sufficiently large \(A>0\),
\[
R=r+Ar^2
\]
has positive-definite full complex Hessian at \(0\). Indeed,
\[
R_{j\bar k}(0)=r_{j\bar k}(0)+2A\,r_j(0)r_{\bar k}(0),
\]
so the added term supplies positivity in the complex normal direction. After shrinking the neighbourhood, \(R\) and \(r\) have the same sign.

The quadratic Taylor expansion can be written
\[
R(z)=2\operatorname{Re}h(z)+H(z)+o(\|z\|^2),
\]
where \(h\) is holomorphic quadratic with \(h(0)=0\), and \(H\) is positive definite. Consequently, for some \(c,\delta>0\),
\[
\operatorname{Re}h(z)\le -c\|z\|^2
\quad\text{on }\overline Y\cap B_\delta.
\]

Choose \(0<\eta<c\delta^2\). Define on \(Y\)
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\operatorname{Re}h(z),-\eta\},&z\in B_\delta,\\
-\eta,&z\notin B_\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
The strict inequality on the artificial sphere gives a collar where the inside formula equals \(-\eta\), so the gluing is valid. The resulting function is bounded, continuous, and plurisubharmonic. Along an interior normal approaching \(q\), it tends to \(0\), while its interior values near \(q\) are negative. Hence it is not locally constant.

This contradicts ingredient 1. Thus an Oka domain, with the definition in the question, cannot have a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point.

### Application in dimension two

If \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\), its Levi form is negative in some nonzero complex-tangential direction at some point. The complex tangent space there is one-dimensional, so the exterior defining function \(r=-\rho\) has strictly positive tangential Levi form: the exterior has a strictly pseudoconvex boundary point.

Therefore
\[
\mathbb C^2\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex},
\]
proving \(2\in N\).

Agent 3 also supplied a stronger local obstruction: for the function above, \(W=\{u>-\eta\}\) is nonempty and bounded. Any entire curve meeting \(W\) has constant \(u\)-composition, stays in \(W\), and is therefore itself constant by coordinatewise Liouville. A nonconstant affine disc in \(W\) cannot satisfy the required entire approximation property.

- An explicit orientation/sign example:

  \]

- For \(r=-\rho\), the corrected function \(r+r^2\) has Hermitian quadratic part \(\operatorname{diag}(2,5)\), holomorphic quadratic term
  \[
  h=-\sqrt3\,w+3w^2,
  \]
  and remainder of degree at least three.
- A later quantitative audit reportedly bounds that remainder by
  \((47/1000)\|z\|^2\) on radius \(1/1000\), yielding
  \(\operatorname{Re}h\le-\|z\|^2/2\) on the local exterior.

These computations audit the algebra; the universal proof still uses standard analytic facts such as subharmonic Liouville and Taylor expansion.

The team initially sought a theorem proving all pseudoconvex compact-domain exteriors Oka. They identified no applicable theorem. Polynomially convex compact-complement results alone do not suffice: smooth bounded pseudoconvex domains need not have polynomially convex closures or Stein neighbourhood bases.

They also sought nonpseudoconvex compact domains with Oka complements, but established none. A proposed rounded annulus family was corrected: some apparently problematic parameters actually give strongly pseudoconvex domains. The explicit quartic above demonstrates nonpseudoconvexity, **not** an Oka complement; in dimension two their proof rules out that complement being Oka.

The full classification remains open in this record, but the supplied target is decisively contradicted.

The proof uses only local Levi-form calculations, plurisubharmonic gluing, subharmonic Liouville, and the exact convex approximation property (CAP) in the question.

### 1. CAP excludes a bounded plurisubharmonic function with a strictly plurisubharmonic patch

Suppose an open set \(Y\) admits a bounded continuous plurisubharmonic function \(u\), smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic on a nonempty open subset \(W\subset Y\).

Choose a nonconstant affine holomorphic disk \(f\), defined near \(Q=\overline{\mathbb D}\), with \(f(Q)\Subset W\). Choose an approximation tolerance sufficiently small that any approximant \(F\) satisfies both:

* \(F(Q)\subset W\);
* \(F\) is nonconstant, since it approximates two separated values of \(f\).

If \(Y\) had the stated CAP, such an entire \(F:\mathbb C\to Y\) would exist. But \(u\circ F\) is bounded and subharmonic on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant. On \(\mathbb D\),
\[
\partial_t\partial_{\bar t}(u\circ F)
=\mathcal L_u(F(t);F'(t)).
\]
Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(W\) forces \(F'=0\) there. The identity theorem makes \(F\) constant everywhere, a contradiction.

This argument needs neither connectedness of \(Y\) nor any smoothness of \(u\) outside \(W\).

### 2. A strictly pseudoconvex boundary point produces such a function

Let \(q\in\partial Y\) be a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point, with local defining function \(r\), oriented so that \(Y=\{r<0\}\).

For sufficiently large \(A>0\),
\[
\widetilde r=r+Ar^2
\]
is strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\), and has the same sign as \(r\) after shrinking the neighborhood. The key identity is
\[
\mathcal L_{\widetilde r}
=(1+2Ar)\mathcal L_r+2A|\partial r|^2.
\]
At the boundary, the added rank-one term supplies positivity in the complex normal direction; tangential positivity is already available.

Choose \(\epsilon>0\) small enough that
\[
\phi=\widetilde r-\epsilon\|z-q\|^2
\]
remains strictly plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of \(\overline{B(q,R)}\), for sufficiently small \(R>0\). On the exterior patch,
\[
\phi<0,\qquad
\phi\le-\epsilon R^2
\quad\text{on }Y\cap\partial B(q,R).
\]
Set \(c=-\epsilon R^2/2\) and define
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\phi(z),c\},&z\in Y\cap B(q,R),\\
c,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,R).
\end{cases}
\]
The strict inequality on the spherical edge ensures valid gluing: locally near that edge, the maximum equals the constant. Thus \(u\) is bounded, continuous, and plurisubharmonic globally on \(Y\).

Moreover, \(\phi(z)\to0\) as \(z\to q\) from \(Y\). Consequently \(\phi>c\) on a nonempty interior patch, where \(u=\phi\) is strictly plurisubharmonic. Step 1 rules out CAP.

Hence **an Oka open set cannot have a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point**.

### 3. Apply the dimension-two orientation

If \(\partial K\subset\mathbb C^2\) is not pseudoconvex, its Levi form is negative on some nonzero complex tangent vector at some \(q\). The complex tangent space has dimension one, so reversing the defining function makes the exterior strictly pseudoconvex at \(q\).

The exterior therefore cannot be Oka. Taking the contrapositive gives
\[
\mathbb C^2\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\Longrightarrow \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex},
\]
which proves \(2\in N\).

The dimension restriction matters: in higher dimensions, one positive exterior tangential direction need not imply strict pseudoconvexity.
